terms.grammar: aequum, neuter of aequus, as the object of facere: “you are not doing what is fair”
evidence: Plaut. Bacch. 1.2.11: tū dīs nec rēctē dīcis: nōn aequum facis (Lewis & Short), s.v. neque

terms.gloss: I accept it, I’m content with it
terms.grammar: aequī, genitive of value, with facere: “I count it as fair”
evidence: Ter. Heaut. 4.5.40: istuc aequī bonīque faciō (Lewis & Short s.v. aequus)
Plaut. Mil. 3.1.189: aequī istuc faciam, it will be all the same to me (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Traupman gives it for “I think that’s fair”. Lewis & Short renders aequī bonīque facere “to regard as fair and reasonable, to put up with, be content with, acquiesce in”, and its examples are all of accepting what one cannot change: it answers “I’m content with it, it’s all the same to me” (see it makes no difference) better than a judgement that something is fair.

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 98, 312, checked against the searchable text and the page image.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
